patient_name: Ward round presentation — new admission with community-acquired pneumonia
chief_complaint: Present an overnight admission to the attending on morning ward rounds in a structured, prioritized format

team_brief.title: Morning ward round: newly admitted community-acquired pneumonia
team_brief.patient: Mr. Daniel Ochieng, 58-year-old man, admitted overnight with community-acquired pneumonia
team_brief.location: Medical ward, morning ward round; the attending has just arrived at the bedside with the team
team_brief.situation: You admitted him overnight and must present the case to the attending for the first time, prioritized and under about three minutes.
background: Three days of fever, productive cough, and pleuritic right-sided chest pain; no recent travel or sick contacts.
Type 2 diabetes on metformin; non-smoker; no prior pneumonia or hospitalizations.
current_status: On admission: temperature 38.6C, HR 108, RR 24, BP 118/76, SpO2 91% on room air.
Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation; white cell count 15.2, CRP elevated; blood cultures pending.
key_data: CURB-65 score calculated at admission was 1 (based on respiratory rate), supporting ward-level care with close monitoring.
Started on empiric antibiotics and 2 L nasal cannula oxygen overnight; saturation improved to 95%.
treatments: IV empiric antibiotics per local community-acquired pneumonia protocol, supplemental oxygen, and antipyretics; blood cultures and sputum culture sent.
team_brief.your_request: Present the case to the attending in a clear, prioritized structure: one-liner, history, exam and investigation findings, assessment with a brief differential, and your proposed plan.
must_include: A concise one-liner with age, sex, and presenting problem.
Relevant history in chronological order, including comorbidities.
Key exam and investigation findings, including vital signs and the chest X-ray result.
A clear assessment naming community-acquired pneumonia first, with at least one alternative considered and ruled less likely.
A logical plan: antibiotics, oxygen, monitoring, and what you are watching for.

kickoff_text: Morning — this is the new admission overnight, right? Go ahead, give me the presentation.
persona_override: You are Dr. Whitfield, the attending physician on morning ward rounds, listening to the learner present Mr. Ochieng, a 58-year-old man admitted overnight with community-acquired pneumonia (fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, right lower lobe consolidation, CURB-65 of 1, hypoxic to 91% on admission now improved on 2L oxygen). If the learner gives a clear one-liner, presents findings in a logical order, states the diagnosis with at least one differential considered, and gives a coherent plan, listen attentively and then ask one focused follow-up question, such as 'What would make you escalate his oxygen or reconsider the diagnosis?' If the presentation is disorganized, rambles through the history before giving a one-liner, or jumps straight to a diagnosis without exam or investigation findings, interrupt politely but firmly: 'Let's start again — give me the one-liner first.' Reward a presentation that stays under about three minutes without you having to ask the learner to shorten it. Stay brisk and time-pressured, as attendings on a busy ward round often are, but not unkind.
learning_objectives: open with a concise one-liner including age, sex, and presenting problem
present history, exam, and investigation findings in a logical, prioritized order
state a clear assessment with the primary diagnosis named first and at least one differential considered
present a structured management plan tied to the assessment
deliver the presentation fluently and within about three minutes without prompting
suggested_questions: This is Mr. Ochieng, a 58-year-old man admitted overnight with community-acquired pneumonia.
He had three days of fever and productive cough with pleuritic chest pain, was hypoxic to 91% on admission, and his chest X-ray showed right lower lobe consolidation.
My assessment is community-acquired pneumonia, CURB-65 of 1, appropriate for ward-level care; I've started empiric antibiotics and oxygen, and I'm watching his oxygen requirement and fever trend.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Structured ward-round case presentation for a newly admitted patient with community-acquired pneumonia
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in standard ward-round presentation structure (one-liner, HPI, exam, investigations, assessment, plan) and IDSA/ATS community-acquired pneumonia principles; local antibiotic protocols apply
core_concepts: A ward-round presentation should open with a one-liner that orients the listener before any detail is given.
Findings should be presented in the order history, exam, investigations, then assessment and plan, not as an unsorted list of facts.
The assessment should name a leading diagnosis first and briefly note why a plausible alternative is less likely, not just list findings.
diagnostic_clues: Fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, focal consolidation on chest X-ray, and elevated inflammatory markers together support community-acquired pneumonia.
A CURB-65 score helps justify the level of care (ward versus intensive monitoring) as part of the assessment.
common_misconceptions: A longer, more detailed presentation is always a better presentation.
Stating the diagnosis is sufficient without mentioning why a reasonable alternative was considered and set aside.
dangerous_errors: Omitting a hypoxic or clinically significant vital sign from the presentation, so the team underestimates severity.
Presenting a plan without linking it to a stated assessment, so the reasoning is not auditable by the team.
management_principles: Use a consistent structure — one-liner, history, exam, investigations, assessment, plan — for every ward-round presentation.
Match the level of care and monitoring plan explicitly to a severity assessment such as CURB-65.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Exact antibiotic choice, dosing, and escalation criteria depend on local community-acquired pneumonia protocols and antimicrobial stewardship guidance.

source_refs.title: ATS/IDSA Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Adults Guidelines
